content: All members of the guideline development group verbally declared their interests, and it was determined that these were not relevant to the guideline on iron supplementation for adult women and adolescent girls. External resource experts also disclosed their interests but did not participate in the deliberation or decision-making processes. The World Health Organization (WHO) Secretariat will continue to monitor research developments in the field of oral iron supplementation for menstruating adult women and adolescent girls, particularly in malaria-endemic and non-malaria-endemic settings. This is especially important for areas where the quality of evidence was rated as low or very low. If the guideline requires an update or if concerns arise regarding its validity, the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development will oversee the update process, adhering to the formal procedures outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. As the guideline approaches its 10-year review period, the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development, in collaboration with internal partners at WHO headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, will conduct a search for new evidence. The guideline on daily iron supplementation for adult women and adolescent girls is supported by moderate-quality evidence for its effects on anemia and iron deficiency. The intervention demonstrated significant improvements in these outcomes. The evidence for its impact on hemoglobin levels is of high quality, although there is currently no evidence available on its effect on iron deficiency anemia. While evidence on gastrointestinal side effects, such as loose or hard stools, is of high quality, the overall evidence for adverse effects or gastrointestinal issues is of low or very low quality. Adherence to the intervention may be a challenge, particularly if it is perceived as non-essential. Limited access to healthcare facilities, especially in rural areas, may exacerbate this issue, leading to inequities in implementation. The benefits of daily iron supplementation include improved hemoglobin levels and a reduced risk of anemia and iron deficiency, which have functional benefits such as enhanced exercise performance. However, potential harms include gastrointestinal effects, such as diarrhea or constipation, with high-quality evidence supporting these risks. There is insufficient data on adverse events or long-term harms, such as overdose, particularly in individuals with adequate iron levels. The cost of implementing the intervention will largely depend on operational challenges rather than the cost of the supplements themselves. Establishing vertical programs for supplementation may be expensive, and health services without preventive care for menstruating women and girls may find the intervention less feasible.
